c.tagline: Ecuador's steamy Pacific port, riverfront Malecón, and gateway to the Galápagos.

taxi.fareNote: Many street taxis do not run the meter for tourists; agree the fare before getting in, or use Uber/InDrive/Cabify for a set price and added safety. Official airport taxis use fixed zone pricing paid at a counter (about $5-8 to downtown).

emergency.note: ECU 911 is Ecuador's single nationwide emergency line connecting police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Avoid south of Portete de Tarqui Ave, El Guasmo and northern suburbs (Kennedy/Alborada).
Muggings even on the Malecón — stay in Samborondón/Puerto Santa Ana.

hood_desc: The central downtown core along the Malecón 2000 riverfront promenade, lined with gardens, museums, an IMAX, malls, and restaurants overlooking the Guayas River; the most convenient, walkable base for first-timers who want the main sights on their doorstep.

Guayaquil's oldest neighborhood and a declared Cultural Heritage site, a colorful hillside of restored 400-year-old colonial houses, art galleries, and cafes climbing the 444 steps of Cerro Santa Ana to a lighthouse with sweeping river views; best for travelers into history and photography.

A leafy middle-class district west of downtown famous for its dining and nightlife, with Victor Emilio Estrada avenue packed with restaurants, bars, cafes, and shops serving everything from ceviche to sushi; a more local, going-out vibe.

An upscale, master-planned residential enclave across the river in La Puntilla, synonymous with luxury: gated communities, high-end malls, riverside restaurants, and modern towers; calm, secure, and car-dependent, favored by affluent locals and long-stay visitors.

A modern redeveloped waterfront district just north of Las Peñas, with a marina, riverside boardwalk, sleek residential towers, hotels, bars, restaurants, and a music museum; a polished, safe-feeling riverfront pocket good for dining and evenings out.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water, as most residents do.

transit.hours: The Metrovía and Aerovía generally run from around 5:00/6:00 AM to about 10:00/11:00 PM daily; there is no late-night service, so ride-hailing apps or taxis cover the overnight hours.
transit.note: Guayaquil has no underground metro; the backbone is the Metrovía bus rapid transit network (three trunk corridors on dedicated lanes with feeder buses), complemented by the Aerovía aerial cable car linking downtown to Durán. Petty theft on crowded buses is common, so keep valuables secure.
transit.pay: The Metrovía BRT charges a flat $0.45 (reduced $0.15 for students/seniors), paid in cash at station turnstiles or with the reloadable 'La Guayaca' card; the Aerovía cable car across the Guayas River to Durán is $0.76. Ordinary city buses are paid in cash (about $0.35) directly to the driver.

Official fixed-zone airport taxi to the city center (~15-25 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; mid-range and upscale restaurants often add a 10% service charge, and rounding up or leaving a little extra for good service is appreciated.

food.name: Encebollado
food.desc: Ecuador's hangover cure: albacore tuna in a cassava and tomato broth under pickled red onion, finished with lime and fried plantain chips.

places.name: La Culata
places.note: Guayaquil institution locals name first for encebollado; go before noon.

places.name: Mercado Central food stalls
places.note: Cheap early-morning bowls served the way dock workers eat them.

places.name: Casa Julian
places.note: Seafood favourite whose encebollado and ceviches both get consistent praise.

food.name: Bolon de verde
food.desc: Ball of mashed green plantain kneaded with pork crackling or cheese, griddled and eaten for breakfast with coffee.

places.name: Cafe de Tere
places.note: The city's benchmark for bolon and tigrillo; queues form and they sell out.

places.name: Cafe de Tere Kennedy
places.note: Second branch with the same breakfast plates, usually less of a wait.

places.name: Mercado Central breakfast counters
places.note: Plantain balls fried to order alongside bolones de queso and coffee.

food.name: Cangrejo criollo
food.desc: Red mangrove crabs steamed with beer, garlic and cumin, dumped on the table with mallets; a weekend ritual, not a quiet meal.

places.name: La Cangrejada
places.note: Big, loud crab-and-beer hall packed with families on Sunday afternoons.

places.name: Red Crab
places.note: Long-running crab specialist, easier for first-timers with table service.

places.name: Mercado Caraguay
places.note: City seafood market where crab comes straight off the boats.

food.name: Arroz con menestra y carne asada
food.desc: The coastal plate of the day: rice, stewed lentil or bean menestra, grilled beef and fried plantain with garlic-lime salsa.

places.name: Lo Nuestro
places.note: Old-house restaurant known for classic Ecuadorian criollo cooking.

places.name: Menestras del Negro
places.note: Reliable everyday version of the plate at low prices across the city.

places.name: Urdesa parrilla strip
places.note: Grill restaurants along Victor Emilio Estrada plate it with charcoal beef.

food.name: Ceviche de camaron
food.desc: Cooked shrimp in tangy tomato and lime leche de tigre with onion and cilantro, served with popcorn, chifles and plantain chips.

places.name: Casa Julian
places.note: Regularly cited for its shrimp ceviche and cazuela de mariscos.

places.name: Mercado Caraguay
places.note: Market cevicherias serve it minutes from the fish counters.

places.name: La Culata
places.note: Same kitchen as the famous encebollado, strong on shrimp and shell ceviches.

food.name: Guatita
food.desc: Tripe simmered in a peanut and potato sauce over rice, a Guayaquil comfort dish usually eaten at lunch or very late at night.

places.name: La Canoa
places.note: Round-the-clock downtown restaurant serving Ecuadorian classics including guatita.

places.name: Lo Nuestro
places.note: Traditional criollo menu where guatita sits beside seco de chivo.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Market kitchens ladle it over rice for a few dollars.

food.name: Pilsener beer
food.desc: Ecuador's everyday lager, brewed in Guayaquil and drunk ice cold in litre bottles, especially with crab.

places.name: La Cangrejada
places.note: Beer and crab arrive together; the pairing the city is built on.

places.name: Red Crab
places.note: Cold litre bottles to cut through the garlic and cumin crab sauce.

places.name: Malecon 2000 riverfront bars
places.note: Open-air terraces on the Guayas for a beer at sunset.

food.name: Batidos de frutas
food.desc: Blended tropical shakes of guanabana, maracuya, naranjilla or mora, made with milk or water at markets and breakfast cafes.

places.name: Mercado Central juice counters
places.note: Rows of blenders working through fruit you will not find at home.

places.name: Cafe de Tere

places.name: La Canoa

landmarks: Malecón 2000
This revitalized 2.5-kilometer riverfront boardwalk along the Guayas River is the city's pride, packed with gardens, monuments, museums, and sweeping river views.
Las Peñas
Guayaquil's oldest neighborhood charms visitors with steep cobblestone streets, colorful colonial houses, and art galleries climbing dramatically up Santa Ana Hill.
Santa Ana Hill (Cerro Santa Ana)
Climbing 444 colorful steps past cafes and murals to a lighthouse summit, this hill rewards visitors with the city's best panoramic view over the river and skyline.
Parque Seminario (Iguana Park)
Dozens of large iguanas roam freely beneath the trees of this unassuming downtown plaza, creating one of Guayaquil's most delightfully unexpected photo opportunities.
La Rotonda
This bronze monument depicts the historic 1822 meeting between Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín, standing as a grand centerpiece along the Malecón waterfront.
Municipal Palace of Guayaquil
This Beaux-Arts government building with its ornate Moorish-style tower is a downtown architectural showpiece, especially striking when illuminated at night.
Metropolitan Cathedral of Guayaquil
Facing Parque Seminario with its neo-Gothic spires and striped facade, this cathedral's ornate interior is a peaceful counterpoint to the surrounding iguana-filled plaza.
Guayaquil Historical Park
This open-air park recreates Ecuador's coastal past with restored haciendas, wildlife reserves, and traditional architecture, offering an immersive escape from the city center.
Guayaquil Skyline
Ecuador's largest city presents a striking modern skyline of glass towers rising along the Guayas River, best appreciated from the Malecón or Santa Ana Hill.
Malecón del Salado
A quieter counterpart to Malecón 2000, this scenic esplanade along the Salado estuary offers boat rides, gardens, and a relaxed local escape from the busy downtown.

train.note: The Guayaquil-Quito railway historically started not in the city but at Durán across the Guayas river, and all passenger services on Ecuador's network were suspended in March 2020 before the operator was liquidated; only short tourist sections in Imbabura and Chimborazo have run since. There is therefore no train service to Guayaquil and no international rail in Ecuador at all. The Aerovía cable car now provides the quick link across the river to Durán that the trains once used, and long-distance travel is by coach or air.

bus.note: The Terminal Terrestre Jaime Roldós Aguilera stands next to the airport about 5 km north of the centre and is linked to town by the Metrovía busway; dozens of companies sell from counters on the upper floors, mostly in cash. Domestic services include Cuenca (3.5-4 hours), Quito (8-9 hours), Salinas and Montañita (2.5 hours). For Peru, coaches take roughly 4-5 hours to the Huaquillas border, where the joint CEBAF post issues both the exit and entry stamps in one stop, then continue to Tumbes, Máncora and Piura; through buses to Lima take around 26-28 hours and should be booked a day or two ahead.

ferry.note: The Port of Guayaquil is Ecuador's largest container and cargo terminal but handles no scheduled passenger sailings, and there is no boat service to the Galápagos - those islands are reached by air from José Joaquín de Olmedo airport. Small lanchas still cross the Guayas from the Malecón to Durán and out to Puná Island, but they are informal river taxis paid at the jetty rather than a ticketed ferry, and the Aerovía cable car has largely replaced the Durán crossing.

half.name: Churute Mangroves Ecological Reserve
half.blurb: Protected mangrove estuary south of the city with canoe trips through channels and howler monkey sightings.

half.name: Puerto El Morro
half.blurb: Fishing village on the Gulf of Guayaquil where boat tours watch a resident pod of bottlenose dolphins.

half.name: Playas (General Villamil)
half.blurb: Pacific coast beach town popular with day-trippers for its long sandy shoreline and seafood shacks.

full.name: Salinas
full.blurb: Pacific resort town at Ecuador's westernmost point, with a malecón, condo towers, and sport-fishing charters.

full.name: Montañita
full.blurb: Surf town on the Pacific coast known for its beach breaks and backpacker nightlife scene.
